summary: Create a Run and bind it as this profile's current Run
usage: corral orchestration run-create [--objective VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: Records are Run (run_<12 hex>), Task (task_<12 hex>) and Dispatch (ctx_<12 hex>), stored as one JSON document under <userData>/runtime/orchestration/state.json. One mutation is one atomic rename, so a task, its attempt and any dependents promoted by the same call commit together or not at all. Durability is the profile's existing promise: process-crash safe, not power-loss safe (no directory fsync, no F_FULLFSYNC). A document that is damaged, foreign or internally inconsistent is storage_corrupt and is never rewritten, truncated or reinitialized; an absent one is simply a new profile.

The current Run is bound per profile, not per calling terminal. --run <id> overrides it for one call without rebinding it. With neither, commands that need a Run fail run_required before any effect and before any receipt is written, and resources.recovery names run-create/run-use.

Task status is pending|ready|dispatched|completed|failed|blocked; Dispatch status is dispatched|completed|failed|unknown. failed means an observed failure only: an absent pane, a replaced PTY, a changed backend generation and an unreachable backend are never turned into failed, and nothing is retried automatically.

A rejected mutation is decided before its receipt exists, so its --request-id stays unspent; borrowed codes request_conflict, outcome_unknown, receipt_capacity and request_expired come from the shared receipt store. Every mutation accepts --request-id r1.<13-digit Unix milliseconds>.<UUID> and mints one when it is omitted, sharing the profile's existing 24-hour receipt store. A replayed id returns the first result with replayed true, the same id with different input is request_conflict, and a receipt that is still pending is outcome_unknown and is never re-executed; an outcome_unknown answer carries stage receipt and a recovery that names run-show/task-list/dispatch-show, never a new --request-id, because the mutation may already be stored. An id the receipt store itself turns away before admission - a timestamp in the future, request_expired, receipt_capacity - is unspent too.
This command group starts nothing and sends nothing to any pane. Dispatch records which pane an attempt is bound to; launching the worker, its messages and its completion are LIFE-410.
run-create always rebinds the current Run to the Run it created.

Reconcile re-observes every open attempt before each orchestration command, once when the runtime starts, and again on dispatch-show for an attempt that is still open: the same generation alive keeps the attempt dispatched and reports terminal.live true; an absent pane, a replaced PTY or a changed backend generation settles it unknown with reason pane_gone|pty_replaced|epoch_changed and leaves the Task dispatched so it can be dispatched again; an unreachable backend records nothing at all and reports observed false with terminal.live unknown. The observation has its own budget - 2000 ms, never more than half of the time the caller has left, and skipped entirely below 250 ms of share - so a backend that never answers cannot hold a read command open; too little time to look is the same as could not look. The runtime-start pass also stops as soon as an orchestration command that is going to run arrives, because that command re-observes under its own deadline; a command rejected by validation never reaches the lane and never cuts it short. A reconcile result is stored by a read command - that record stands whether the read then succeeds or fails - or by the mutation it travels with; a rejected mutation writes nothing at all. Only reconcile creates unknown, and it never creates failed.

The manual table is dispatched -> completed|failed, anything except completed -> blocked, and blocked -> ready|pending. ready -> dispatched belongs to the dispatch command alone, and completed is terminal. An open attempt additionally refuses -> blocked: settle it with completed|failed, or let reconcile close it once its pane is gone, so a live worker is never left with an attempt no command can end. Anything else is illegal_transition with the allowed set in resources.

For a request that passes validation the checks run in a fixed order and every rejection is effect-free: --expected-version mismatch is version_conflict, then an illegal transition is illegal_transition, then a --dispatch that is not the open attempt is stale_dispatch. Settling a Task that is already settled is therefore illegal_transition even when the caller names the attempt that settled it, while naming a superseded attempt of a still-open Task is stale_dispatch. Flag validation runs before all of them, so --status dispatched is illegal_transition whatever the other flags say.

Omitting --dispatch settles whichever attempt is open, which is how a human settles a Task whose attempt reconcile already marked unknown. blocked -> ready additionally requires every dependency completed; blocked -> pending is always available.

The agent block is an observation made at dispatch time and is never refreshed: a pane dispatched while its provider was still launching keeps phase launching and resolvedModel null for the life of the record. Read the pane itself with terminal show for its current state. Nothing is sent to the pane and no agent is started.

summary: Show one attempt and re-observe the pane it is bound to
usage: corral orchestration dispatch-show [--id VALUE] [--task VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: Records are Run (run_<12 hex>), Task (task_<12 hex>) and Dispatch (ctx_<12 hex>), stored as one JSON document under <userData>/runtime/orchestration/state.json. One mutation is one atomic rename, so a task, its attempt and any dependents promoted by the same call commit together or not at all. Durability is the profile's existing promise: process-crash safe, not power-loss safe (no directory fsync, no F_FULLFSYNC). A document that is damaged, foreign or internally inconsistent is storage_corrupt and is never rewritten, truncated or reinitialized; an absent one is simply a new profile.

The current Run is bound per profile, not per calling terminal. --run <id> overrides it for one call without rebinding it. With neither, commands that need a Run fail run_required before any effect and before any receipt is written, and resources.recovery names run-create/run-use.

Task status is pending|ready|dispatched|completed|failed|blocked; Dispatch status is dispatched|completed|failed|unknown. failed means an observed failure only: an absent pane, a replaced PTY, a changed backend generation and an unreachable backend are never turned into failed, and nothing is retried automatically.
This command group starts nothing and sends nothing to any pane. Dispatch records which pane an attempt is bound to; launching the worker, its messages and its completion are LIFE-410.
Give exactly one of --id or --task; --task selects that Task's most recent attempt. Neither is dispatch_not_found.

Reconcile re-observes every open attempt before each orchestration command, once when the runtime starts, and again on dispatch-show for an attempt that is still open: the same generation alive keeps the attempt dispatched and reports terminal.live true; an absent pane, a replaced PTY or a changed backend generation settles it unknown with reason pane_gone|pty_replaced|epoch_changed and leaves the Task dispatched so it can be dispatched again; an unreachable backend records nothing at all and reports observed false with terminal.live unknown. The observation has its own budget - 2000 ms, never more than half of the time the caller has left, and skipped entirely below 250 ms of share - so a backend that never answers cannot hold a read command open; too little time to look is the same as could not look. The runtime-start pass also stops as soon as an orchestration command that is going to run arrives, because that command re-observes under its own deadline; a command rejected by validation never reaches the lane and never cuts it short. A reconcile result is stored by a read command - that record stands whether the read then succeeds or fails - or by the mutation it travels with; a rejected mutation writes nothing at all. Only reconcile creates unknown, and it never creates failed.

For an attempt that was still open when the call started the response's terminal block is the observation this call made (source observation), including the one that settles it unknown; for an attempt that was already settled this call makes no observation of its own and the block repeats the stored reconcile with live null and source record - the sweep that precedes every command still contacts the backend once if another attempt is open. The record's reconcile block is the last observation that changed something, with the runtime instance that recorded it. Repeating the call therefore leaves the stored document byte-identical.

summary: Start or re-use a worker pane for a Task and deliver its preamble exactly once
usage: corral orchestration worker-start [--task VALUE] [--terminal VALUE] [--agent VALUE] [--model VALUE] [--effort VALUE] [--advisor VALUE] [--worktree VALUE] [--title VALUE] [--spec-file VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
examples: corral orchestration worker-start --task task_0123456789ab --agent claude --model opus --worktree /path/to/worktree --timeout-ms 120000 --json
notes: Exactly one of --terminal (re-use a pane corral already started an agent in) or --agent claude|codex|grok with --worktree (start one). A re-used pane keeps the agent it was started with, so --model, --effort, --advisor and --worktree are refused with --terminal, and a pane that carries no corral-managed agent is agent_not_found with no effect.

One line is typed into the pane immediately before the preamble is pasted into it - a provider that receives a message made entirely of pasted text refuses to act on it as a possible injection. That line carries no newline, so the Enter that submits is the prompt's own: a Dispatch is one Enter and one promptRequestId, and that is what once counts. The typed line and the paste are two effects, and each is recorded before it is made - worker.lead and worker.prompt. Each record is a claim taken inside the document lane and written only while the key is still null, so the run that writes it is the only run that makes that effect: a Dispatch types at most one lead and submits at most one body in any race, and two runs resuming the same attempt at once cannot both act on the null they each planned from. A claim is given back only when the child refused before any effect and said so; a failure carrying no outcome, or one that says unknown, leaves the record standing because the text may already have reached the pane. corral cannot clear a pane's input line, so when an earlier run typed the lead the answer lists an input_line entry in residualResources for a person to clear - from the record, not from a screen. The lead block beside it is a diagnostic and nothing branches on it: present is true when the lead's text is somewhere on the screen and null otherwise, never false, because corral cannot prove an input line is clear and no value of it ever causes a line to be typed.

The composition is terminal create --agent, then the Dispatch record, then terminal wait --for agent-ready, then terminal prompt with the preamble and the TASK body. The attempt is created before the body is built because the preamble names it. Each stage reports separately in stages and effects; a stage that fails leaves the earlier ones in place and names them in residualResources rather than undoing them.

The submission is judged, not assumed. state ready is reported only when terminal prompt answered outcome completed with its wait satisfied, or when this exact body was found in the provider's record exactly once - which reaches corral either as the duplicate pre-check refusing a new submission with matchCount 1, or as the recorded receipt of an earlier run's submission with record.matchCount 1. The count is read through the receipt wrapper as well as beside it, because terminal prompt runs inside the receipt store and a refusal that crosses it carries the child's own resources under detail. Anything else - outcome unknown, an unmet wait, queue acceptance, or a count of two or more - is state incomplete at stage dispatch_input_unconfirmed with stages.input.status unknown: the body may well have arrived, promptRequestId stays null, and the attempt stays resumable. Two matching submissions are not one confirmed delivery; they are a one-input rule already broken for that pane, and they are reported rather than promoted. A Dispatch that never reached the pane is never reported as ready.

The preamble reaches a pane exactly once per Dispatch. The same --request-id replays the stored result and submits nothing; a different id while the attempt is open and its preamble delivered is task_not_startable with reason dispatch_active. An attempt whose input stage never completed - a trust dialog, a deadline, a submission whose arrival was never seen - is the one exception: calling worker-start again for that Task resumes it into the same pane and the same Dispatch. What that resume believes is the Dispatch's record and the receipt of the request id it names, never the pane's screen. A completed receipt is the child's own answer and the resume follows it as it stands: a satisfied wait, or record.unavailableReason null - which terminal prompt writes only for one proven match on a cursor it had not lost - is a delivery this run observed rather than made. A receipt that is pending or missing means the effect may have happened and was never seen, and a completed one carrying any unavailableReason means the count beside it is not proof in either direction: a single match on an invalidated cursor is unknown at the source, and a count of zero is also what a provider that had not written its record by the deadline answers. Both stop at stage dispatch_input_unprovable with state incomplete, submitting nothing, naming the request id, the reason, the count and the pane to read; a receipt that cannot be read at all stops there too with reason receipt_unreadable. A resume does not count again, so an attempt does not leave that state on its own - a person reads the pane and ends the attempt with worker-stop, because a new Dispatch on the same pane carries a different dispatch id and would put the same body in a second time.

A worker pane inherits its environment from the backend, never from corral, so the preamble spells every command with this runtime socket. The TASK body is --spec-file when given and the Task spec otherwise, and it must be at most 49152 bytes so the preamble fits in one submission.

A resume delivers the body the Dispatch was created against and nothing else. The digest of that body is recorded when the Dispatch is created, before anything is sent, and it is the digest - not the flags on the command line - that decides what a resume delivers. An attempt made from the Task spec resumes from the Task, and a --spec-file left on the line is listed in ignoredOptions without being opened at all, so a path that has since gone away cannot refuse a resume it has nothing to do with. Only when the Task no longer explains the stored digest is the named file read, and then it is read to be compared: the same body resumes, a changed one is preamble_mismatch with no effect. A new attempt is a different question - there the file is the body, so an unreadable one is invalid_argument. launch reports created, reused or resumed, and ignoredOptions lists the options that could not take effect because the attempt already has both a pane and a body.

Re-using a pane transfers ownership: the settled attempt that owned it becomes borrowed and names the new attempt in ownershipTransferredTo, so releasing the old attempt no longer closes a pane the new worker is using. A retained attempt still owns its pane - only a released release ends ownership - so it hands it over too. Whether a pane is busy is a separate question from who may close it: any open attempt bound to that pane refuses the re-use with dispatch_active, borrowed panes included. Both questions are asked again inside the write itself, on the document that write is made on, so two worker-start calls racing for one pane leave one attempt and one owner rather than two - a refusal found there is a stage failure on dispatch rather than a preflight rejection, because a race is not something preflight can foresee. A pane no settled attempt owns - one a person started with terminal create --agent - is borrowed and is never closed by corral.

Every mutation accepts --request-id r1.<13-digit Unix milliseconds>.<UUID> and mints one when it is omitted, sharing the profile 24-hour receipt store. A replayed id returns the first result with replayed true, the same id with different input is request_conflict, and a receipt still pending is outcome_unknown and is never re-executed. Rejections this module can foresee are raised before the receipt exists, so a refused call leaves its id unspent and the stored bytes untouched.

summary: List the workers of a Run with their ownership and recovery state
usage: corral orchestration worker-list [--run VALUE] [--status VALUE] [--limit VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: One row per attempt that was started as a worker, newest first. workerState is working while the attempt is open, reported once a worker_done settled it, settled when a person did, and unknown when reconcile could no longer observe its pane.

The worker block names launch, ownership, originDispatchId, ownershipTransferredTo, lastHeartbeatAt, capabilityRevokedAt and the retain and release records. --status filters on the Dispatch status and takes only a Dispatch word - dispatched, completed, failed or unknown. The Task words ready and blocked are refused here rather than accepted into a filter no row could ever match.

summary: Show one worker: its attempt, ownership, capability and live pane
usage: corral orchestration worker-show [--dispatch VALUE] [--task VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: Exactly one of --dispatch or --task; --task reports the most recent attempt. The pane is observed either way: observation.live answers whether the pane is there right now, and observation.record carries the reconcile reason and time the record already held. A settled attempt is still worth observing - whether its pane survived it is the difference between a transcript still open in front of you and nothing left to read - and the observation changes nothing: worker-show reconciles nothing, settles nothing, and reports the Task the document already held.

messageCounts and lastMessage summarise what this attempt sent. This is the recovery command for a release or stop whose close could not be confirmed; corral does not suggest working around it with terminal close.

summary: Read the terminal output of a worker pane
usage: corral orchestration worker-read [--dispatch VALUE] [--cursor VALUE] [--limit VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--screen] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: A pass-through of terminal read against the pane the Dispatch is bound to, so the cursor is the terminal cursor and stays valid across calls. source is terminal: corral installs no provider hook and reads no transcript.
Nothing is stored. Reading a worker never changes the record.

summary: Send a message to the Run mailbox; worker_done also settles the attempt
usage: corral orchestration send [--type VALUE] [--subject VALUE] [--body VALUE] [--payload VALUE] [--task-id VALUE] [--dispatch-id VALUE] [--outcome VALUE] [--phase VALUE] [--files-modified VALUE] [--report-path VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
examples: corral orchestration send --type worker_done --subject "done" --body "…" --task-id task_0123456789ab --dispatch-id ctx_0123456789ab --outcome succeeded --json
corral orchestration send --type heartbeat --subject alive --task-id task_0123456789ab --dispatch-id ctx_0123456789ab --phase implementing --json
notes: --type worker_done|heartbeat|escalation are worker reports and require --task-id and --dispatch-id. --type status is the one type either side sends: with --task-id and --dispatch-id it is that worker's status and is verified like any other worker report, with neither it is a note on the Run. One of the two without the other is refused.

worker_done requires --outcome succeeded|failed and settles the Task and the attempt through the same transition table task-update uses, with settledBy worker_done: succeeded becomes completed and promotes any dependents, failed becomes failed. Do not follow it with task-update. Storing the message and settling the attempt is one write, so the two can never disagree.

Whether a report can be accepted at all - the transition it would make, and the mailbox's own capacity - is computed before the receipt is admitted. A refused worker_done therefore leaves the receipt directory byte for byte as it was, and its --request-id unspent.
A heartbeat updates lastHeartbeatAt. corral records it and never judges liveness by it.

A worker report (send --type worker_done|heartbeat|escalation, send --type status naming an attempt, and ask) names --task-id and --dispatch-id and is accepted only from the pane that Dispatch was bound to. The CLI reads HERDR_PANE_ID and HERDR_SESSION from the pane shell herdr starts and sends them beside the flags; the runtime compares them with the Dispatch target and then looks at the pane itself, because the stored ids and the caller's environment still agree after the pane they name is gone. A call from another pane or from outside a pane is sender_mismatch, a pane that is gone is stale_dispatch, a pane answering with a different pty or epoch and a pane corral cannot observe at all are sender_mismatch, a superseded attempt is stale_dispatch, a second worker_done is illegal_transition, and an attempt that was stopped, abandoned or released is capability_revoked. Every one of those stores nothing at all - worker_done included, which is refused rather than recorded when the pane cannot be observed. sessionVerified in the answer says whether the session half of the comparison was made at all: an attempt started where CORRAL_SESSION was unset recorded no session, so the pane id stands alone. A claude session moved to the background (`←`, `/bg`) runs in Claude Code's account-wide daemon, whose HERDR_* are those of the pane that first started the daemon, so it can never pass the pane comparison; the CLI also sends CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, and when the pane comparison fails the runtime admits the call if that id is the claude session corral minted for the Dispatch's pane or one it continued in — the same continued-in chain terminal show follows (agent.sessionRecord.continuedIn), read from the record files of the minted id the Dispatch froze (found by that id under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR's projects; not exactly one file is no chain), with no backend round trip, so it does not need the pane. Every later check still applies: the pane must be observed live (a pane that is gone is stale_dispatch for the background session too, a replaced pane is sender_mismatch), and revocation, supersession and a second worker_done answer as above. The chain is a claude proof only: a codex or grok attempt, an attempt with no minted session, an id outside the chain or in another Dispatch's chain are sender_mismatch, and so is a background session after /clear, whose new id no continued-in names. proof in the answer is pane or session_chain; an attempt admitted on the chain is never sessionVerified. The session id is what the caller's environment says, like the pane id: confusion-proof, not authentication. One gap predates the chain: the daemon's first pane is whichever pane started Claude Code's daemon, so if that happens to be another Dispatch's pane, a background session that names that other Dispatch is admitted on the pane proof. This is proof against confusion, not authentication: the trust boundary is the 0600 runtime socket, and coordinator-side commands carry no proof for that reason.

Capability lifetime is not process lifetime. Settling, worker-stop, worker-abandon and worker-release all record capabilityRevokedAt, and the first revocation is the one kept. A worker whose pane is still alive can therefore be refused, which is the point: the record says the attempt ended.

Messages live in the Run mailbox inside the same state.json the records use, so storing a report and settling the attempt it ends is one atomic rename. Ids are msg_<12 hex> and delivery_<12 hex>; sequence is monotone within a Run and is what FIFO order means. A Run holds at most 10000 messages and a body at most 65536 bytes; reaching the ceiling is message_capacity, and corral never deletes a stored message to make room.

Every mutation accepts --request-id r1.<13-digit Unix milliseconds>.<UUID> and mints one when it is omitted, sharing the profile 24-hour receipt store. A replayed id returns the first result with replayed true, the same id with different input is request_conflict, and a receipt still pending is outcome_unknown and is never re-executed. Rejections this module can foresee are raised before the receipt exists, so a refused call leaves its id unspent and the stored bytes untouched.

summary: Ask the coordinator a question and block until it is answered

notes: Exactly one of --question (ask a new one) or --resume <msg id> (keep waiting for one already asked). The question is stored durably before the wait begins, so a timeout, a cancelled client or a runtime restart all leave it answerable: --resume never creates a second question, and a question that has already been answered returns its answer at once.

A deadline is a normal answer, not an error: state pending with the messageId and a resumeCommand to run instead of asking again. An answered question returns state answered with the reply body. --timeout-ms is at most 600000, matching what a Claude Code Bash call can actually spend.

The lane is not held while waiting, so asking does not block the coordinator that has to answer. The mailbox's own ceiling is a refusal like any other and is decided before the receipt exists: a Run already holding 10000 messages answers message_capacity with the request id unspent, for a question exactly as for a report or a coordinator status.

This is proof against confusion, not authentication: the trust boundary is the 0600 runtime socket, and coordinator-side commands carry no proof for that reason.

summary: Answer one question a worker asked
usage: corral orchestration reply [--id VALUE] [--body VALUE] [--subject VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
examples: corral orchestration reply --id msg_0123456789ab --body "use the second one" --json
notes: --id names the question. An id no message carries is message_not_found. A message that is not a question is not_a_question and a question that already has an answer is already_answered; both store nothing, so a second reply can never overwrite an answer the worker may already have read.
The reply is stored as its own message addressed to the asker and is never part of a check batch.

Every mutation accepts --request-id r1.<13-digit Unix milliseconds>.<UUID> and mints one when it is omitted, sharing the profile 24-hour receipt store. summary: Take the next batch of mailbox messages, acknowledge the previous one, and optionally wait
usage: corral orchestration check [--ack VALUE] [--types VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--block] [--peek] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: A Run has at most one outstanding Delivery. check hands over the oldest undelivered messages that match --types, at most 50, in sequence order, and keeps handing back that same batch with deliveryReplayed true until it is acknowledged - a message that arrives in the meantime is never mixed into it.

--ack accepts only the Delivery that is currently outstanding. An id already acknowledged, one from an earlier batch, or one that never existed is delivery_stale and changes nothing. With --block the acknowledgement happens once, before the wait begins, not on every poll. --peek reports what the next batch would hold without creating a Delivery.

--block waits for a message and reports count 0 with timedOut true when the deadline passes, which is a normal answer rather than an error. --timeout-ms is at most 600000. deliveryReplayed describes the batch; the receipt field replayed describes the --request-id.
--types defaults to every deliverable type (worker_done, heartbeat, escalation, status, question). A reply belongs to the worker that asked and is never delivered here.

Orchestration commands serialize on one in-process lane around each read-compute-write of the single document. check and ask drop that lane while they wait, so a coordinator blocked in check --block never blocks the worker_done it is waiting for.

summary: List mailbox messages without consuming them
usage: corral orchestration inbox [--run VALUE] [--limit VALUE] [--type VALUE] [--unread] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: A read. It creates no Delivery, acknowledges nothing, and leaves the record exactly as it was. --unread lists messages that have not been acknowledged.
outstandingDeliveryId names the batch check is waiting to have acknowledged, if there is one.

summary: Report what the receipt store knows about one request id
usage: corral orchestration request-show [--id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: completed means the request ran and its result is stored, so the same id replays it. pending means the id was admitted and its outcome was never recorded: it may have taken effect, and corral will not re-execute it. released means the request was refused before its effect began, so the id was given back: within the runtime that refused it the same id is judged afresh, and after a restart it answers outcome_unknown instead.

absent means no receipt is stored, which is not proof that nothing happened - the id may never have been admitted, or its receipt may have expired after 24 hours. The interpretation field says so in the answer itself.
A retry in corral is the same --request-id sent again; there is no separate retry flag.

summary: Declare that a worker pane is to be kept
usage: corral orchestration worker-retain [--dispatch VALUE] [--reason VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: Intent only: no process is touched. --reason is user_requested (the default) or user_takeover, which is how a person says they have taken the pane over - corral never detects that on its own, because it has no GUI to detect it from.
The next worker-release honours the retain once, reports retained with this reason, and clears it; a further worker-release then judges the pane on its own merits.

Every mutation accepts --request-id r1.<13-digit Unix milliseconds>.<UUID> and mints one when it is omitted, sharing the profile 24-hour receipt store. A replayed id returns the first result with replayed true, the same id with different input is request_conflict, and a receipt still pending is outcome_unknown and is never re-executed. Rejections this module can foresee are raised before the receipt exists, so a refused call leaves its id unspent and the stored bytes untouched.

summary: Release a finished worker, closing only a pane this attempt can prove it owns
usage: corral orchestration worker-release [--dispatch VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: The attempt has to have ended: an open one is dispatch_active with no effect, and worker-stop is the command that cancels it.

released happens only when this attempt owns the pane and the pane observed immediately before the close is the same generation. Everything else is retained with a reason and processAction none: borrowed, user_requested or user_takeover, pane_gone, identity_unproven when the PTY or the backend generation moved, observation_failed when corral could not look.

The ownership decision and the close happen in the same lane hold, with a fresh observation taken immediately before the close, so the pane that is closed is the pane that was judged. A close whose effect could not be observed is release.state unknown; worker-show is the recovery, not a second close.
Releasing an already released attempt answers from the record and writes nothing.

Capability lifetime is not process lifetime. Settling, worker-stop, worker-abandon and worker-release all record capabilityRevokedAt, and the first revocation is the one kept. A worker whose pane is still alive can therefore be refused, which is the point: the record says the attempt ended.

Rejections this module can foresee are raised before the receipt exists, so a refused call leaves its id unspent and the stored bytes untouched.

summary: Cancel a running worker: close its pane and settle the attempt failed
usage: corral orchestration worker-stop [--dispatch VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: The attempt has to be open - an attempt that already ended is dispatch_not_active, with worker-release as the recovery - this attempt has to own the pane, and the pane observed right now has to be the same generation. Anything weaker is identity_unproven and does nothing at all - a stop that might have closed the wrong pane is worse than a stop that refused.

On success the pane is closed and the Task and the attempt are settled failed with reason worker_stopped, and the capability is revoked in the same write. A close corral could not confirm still settles the attempt, with release.state unknown and worker-show as the recovery.

Capability lifetime is not process lifetime. Settling, worker-stop, worker-abandon and worker-release all record capabilityRevokedAt, and the first revocation is the one kept. A worker whose pane is still alive can therefore be refused, which is the point: the record says the attempt ended.

Every mutation accepts --request-id r1.<13-digit Unix milliseconds>.<UUID> and mints one when it is omitted, sharing the profile 24-hour receipt store. A replayed id returns the first result with replayed true, the same id with different input is request_conflict, and a receipt still pending is outcome_unknown and is never re-executed. Rejections this module can foresee are raised before the receipt exists, so a refused call leaves its id unspent and the stored bytes untouched.

summary: Give up on a running worker without touching its process
usage: corral orchestration worker-abandon [--dispatch VALUE] [--run VALUE] [--request-id VALUE] [--help] [--json] [--timeout-ms VALUE] [--socket VALUE] [--instance VALUE]
notes: No process action at all: corral does not look at the pane and does not close it. The Task and the attempt are settled failed with reason abandoned, the capability is revoked, and the resource is recorded as retained with reason abandoned.
Use it when the worker is unreachable or must be left alone; worker-stop is the one that closes the pane.
